events.title: Rise of Phoenician Civilization
events.description: Lebanon's coast (ancient Phoenicia) saw emergence of city-states like Byblos, Tyre and Sidon. Phoenicians were great sailors and merchants, establishing Mediterranean trade networks, colonies as far as Carthage and Spain. They invented alphabetic writing, becoming the basis for Greek and Latin alphabets, profoundly influencing Western civilization.

events.title: Tyre Golden Age
events.description: Tyre became most important Phoenician city-state, reaching zenith under Hiram I. Hiram cooperated with Israel's King Solomon, providing cedar wood and craftsmen to build Jerusalem Temple. Tyre established Mediterranean trade empire, famous for purple dye (Tyrian purple).

events.title: Alexander's Siege of Tyre
events.description: Alexander the Great besieged island city of Tyre for 7 months. Tyre resisted stubbornly, but Alexander built causeway connecting mainland, finally capturing city. Siege demonstrated Alexander's military genius and Tyre's resistance spirit. Lebanon entered Hellenistic period.

events.title: Roman Rule
events.description: Rome conquered Phoenicia, Lebanon became part of Roman Syria province. Roman rule brought peace and prosperity to Lebanon. Beirut (Berytus) became important legal center with famous law school. Baalbek built magnificent Roman temples.

events.title: Baalbek Temple Construction
events.description: Rome built massive temple complex in Baalbek (ancient Heliopolis, City of Sun), dedicated to Jupiter, Bacchus and Venus. Baalbek temples among most magnificent Roman Empire architecture, using enormous stone blocks, still standing today, becoming Lebanon's most important ancient site.

events.title: Christian Period
events.description: Lebanon became part of Byzantine Empire, Christianity flourished. Maronite Christians formed unique community in Lebanese mountains. Early Church established monasteries and theological centers in Lebanon.

events.title: Arab Conquest
events.description: Arab Muslims conquered Lebanon. Lebanon gradually Islamized, but Maronite Christians and other Christian sects maintained autonomy in mountains. Lebanon became part of Umayyad and later Abbasid Caliphate.

events.title: Druze Arrival
events.description: Druze religious community migrated from Egypt into Lebanese mountains, coexisting with Maronite Christians. Druze is mystical religion branched from Shia Islam, faith kept secret. Druze and Maronite coexistence shaped Lebanon's religious pluralism.

events.title: Crusader Rule
events.description: Crusaders conquered Lebanese coast, establishing County of Tripoli and part of Kingdom of Jerusalem. Maronite Christians allied with Crusaders, establishing enduring ties with West. Crusaders built castles like Byblos and Sidon fortresses.

events.title: Mamluk Conquest
events.description: Mamluks captured Lebanon from Crusaders, ending Crusader rule. Mamluk Sultanate ruled Lebanon for over two centuries. During this period Lebanon relatively marginalized.

events.title: Ottoman Conquest
events.description: Ottoman Empire conquered Lebanon, ruling for 400 years. Ottomans adopted indirect rule, governing through local feudal lords (emirs). Lebanese mountains enjoyed considerable autonomy, Maronite and Druze lords ruled respective communities.

events.title: Ma'an Family Rule
events.description: Druze Ma'an family ruled Lebanese mountains, most famous being Fakhreddine II (1590-1635). Fakhreddine expanded territory, established trade ties with Europe, promoted economic development. But he was eventually executed by Ottoman Sultan.

events.title: Shihab Family Rule
events.description: Shihab family (initially Druze, later converted to Christianity) ruled Mount Lebanon. Bashir II (1788-1840) was most famous ruler, building Beiteddine Palace, consolidating power. But he chose wrong side in Egyptian-Ottoman conflict, was exiled.

events.title: Egyptian Occupation
events.description: Egyptian governor Muhammad Ali conquered Lebanon, implementing modernization reforms including conscription. Conscription policy triggered Druze and Maronite rebellion. European powers intervened, forced Egypt to withdraw, Ottoman restored rule.

events.title: Maronite-Druze Conflict
events.description: Sectarian violence erupted in Mount Lebanon between Maronite Christians and Druze, leading to thousands of Maronite deaths. Violence spread to Damascus, causing more Christian deaths. France sent troops to intervene. This crisis led to establishment of Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate.

events.title: Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate
events.description: Under European powers' pressure, Ottomans established Mount Lebanon special autonomous district (Mutasarrifate), administered by Christian governor, guaranteed by Europe. This arrangement brought relative peace and prosperity, lasting until WWI.

events.title: Great Famine
events.description: During WWI, Lebanon suffered devastating famine, about 200,000 people (one-third of population) died. Famine caused by Ottoman blockade, locusts, requisitions and Allied naval blockade. This disaster deeply imprinted on Lebanese collective memory.

events.title: Greater Lebanon Declared
events.description: After French occupation, French General Gouraud declared establishment of 'Greater Lebanon', expanding Mount Lebanon to include Beirut, Tripoli, Sidon and Bekaa Valley. This created modern Lebanon's borders, but also incorporated large Muslim population, sowing seeds of sectarian conflict.

events.title: French Mandate
events.description: League of Nations granted France mandate over Lebanon. France promoted confessional system, allocating political power by religion. This system reinforced sectarian identity, becoming foundation and curse of Lebanese politics. France developed infrastructure and education, but also suppressed nationalism.

events.title: Lebanese Republic Constitution
events.description: France drafted Lebanese constitution, establishing republic, but retained French control. Constitution established parliamentary system, though not explicitly stated, seats actually allocated by sect. This laid foundation for later National Pact.

events.title: Independence and National Pact
events.description: Lebanon gained independence under Bechara El Khoury and Riad al-Solh. The two leaders reached the unwritten National Pact: president must be Maronite Christian, PM Sunni Muslim, speaker Shia Muslim. Parliament seats distributed 6:5 ratio Christian to Muslim. This confessional system dominates Lebanese politics to this day.

events.title: Arab-Israeli War and Palestinian Refugees
events.description: First Arab-Israeli War led to approximately 100,000 Palestinian refugees fleeing to Lebanon. This significantly changed Lebanon's demographic balance, planting seeds for future conflicts. Palestinian refugee camps established in Lebanon.

events.title: Golden Age
events.description: Lebanon experienced 'golden age' of prosperity and cultural flourishing. Beirut became 'Paris of the East', regional financial and cultural center. Banking, commerce and tourism thrived. French and Arab culture blended, creating unique cosmopolitan atmosphere. But prosperity masked underlying sectarian and class tensions.

events.title: 1958 Crisis
events.description: Political crisis triggered by President Chamoun's pro-Western policies and possible re-election bid. Muslim and leftist opposition demanded pan-Arab alignment. US Marines landed to support government. Crisis ended with compromise: Fouad Chehab elected president, pursuing neutral policy.

events.title: Six-Day War Aftermath
events.description: Israel's 1967 victory led to more Palestinian refugees and PLO strengthening. Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon intensified, increasing tensions with Lebanese Christians. Lebanon's sovereignty gradually eroded.

events.title: PLO Moves to Lebanon
events.description: After 'Black September' PLO expulsion from Jordan, PLO leadership and armed fighters relocated to Lebanon. PLO established 'state within a state' in Palestinian camps and South Lebanon. This further destabilized Lebanon, leading to Israeli attacks.

events.title: Civil War Erupts
events.description: Maronite Phalangist militia attacked a bus carrying Palestinians, killing 27. This incident triggered the Lebanese Civil War, lasting 15 years. The war was complex sectarian, class and regional conflict involving multiple Lebanese factions, PLO, Syria, Israel and other external forces.

events.title: Syrian Military Intervention
events.description: As civil war escalated, Syria sent troops into Lebanon at Lebanese Christian request. Syrian intervention reversed Palestinian and leftist victories. Syria became Lebanon's de facto ruler, occupying Lebanon for 29 years. Syrian presence controversial, seen as stabilizer by some, occupier by others.

events.title: Israel Invades South Lebanon
events.description: After PLO terrorists attacked Israeli bus killing 38, Israel launched Operation Litani, invading South Lebanon. Israel occupied area up to Litani River. Under international pressure, Israel withdrew but established South Lebanon Army (SLA) proxy militia in 'security zone'. UN peacekeeping force UNIFIL deployed.

events.title: Israeli Large-Scale Invasion
events.description: Israel launched Operation Peace for Galilee, massive invasion of Lebanon, aiming to eliminate PLO. Israeli forces advanced to Beirut, besieging West Beirut. After bloody siege, PLO agreed to leave Lebanon for Tunisia.

events.title: Bachir Gemayel Elected President
events.description: Phalangist leader Bachir Gemayel elected president with Israeli support. Bachir was charismatic young Maronite leader, aimed to restore Christian dominance and reach peace with Israel. But before taking office, he was assassinated in party headquarters bomb explosion.

events.title: Sabra and Shatila Massacre
events.description: After Bachir Gemayel's assassination, Maronite Phalangist militia entered Sabra and Shatila refugee camps with Israeli complicity, massacring hundreds to thousands of Palestinian civilians. This massacre shocked the world, Israel was accused of complicity, Defense Minister Sharon was forced to resign.

events.title: US Embassy Bombing
events.description: Suicide bomber attacked US Embassy in Beirut, killing 63 including 17 Americans. This was first major suicide bombing in Lebanon, demonstrating rise of Shia militant groups and US target status in civil war. Attack blamed on Hezbollah or related groups.

events.title: Beirut Barracks Bombing
events.description: Two suicide truck bombs simultaneously attacked US and French barracks in Beirut, killing 241 US Marines and 58 French paratroopers. This was one of deadliest attacks on US since WWII. Attacks prompted US and France to withdraw from Lebanon in early 1984.

events.title: Israel Withdraws from Most of Lebanon
events.description: Under resistance and casualties pressure, Israel withdrew from most of Lebanon, retaining only South Lebanon security zone. Israeli occupation of south continued until 2000. Withdrawal acknowledged Israel's failure to eliminate PLO and achieve peace.

events.title: Western Hostage Crisis
events.description: Pro-Iranian Shia groups (mainly Hezbollah and Islamic Jihad) kidnapped dozens of Westerners including journalists, diplomats and academics, holding them hostage for years. Most famous was AP journalist Terry Anderson held 7 years. Hostage crisis highlighted Western powerlessness and made Hezbollah internationally notorious.

events.title: Dual Government Crisis
events.description: At end of President Gemayel's term, parliament failed to elect successor due to Syrian opposition. Gemayel appointed army commander Michel Aoun as military government PM. But parliament elected Muslim PM Selim al-Hoss, forming dual governments. Aoun launched 'liberation war' against Syria, escalating conflict, finally defeated by Syrian army.

events.title: Taif Agreement
events.description: Lebanese MPs reached agreement in Saudi Taif, ending civil war. Agreement adjusted power distribution, Christian-Muslim parliament seats changed to 5:5, weakened president powers, strengthened PM and speaker. Agreement confirmed Syria's special role. After implementation in 1990, civil war officially ended.

events.title: Civil War Ends
events.description: After Taif Agreement implementation, Lebanese army (with Syrian support) defeated General Aoun, forcing him to flee to French embassy and later exile. This marked official end of 15-year civil war. War killed about 120,000-150,000, displaced hundreds of thousands, destroyed infrastructure. Syria became dominant force in Lebanon.

events.title: Rafic Hariri First Term as PM
events.description: Billionaire businessman Rafic Hariri became PM, began massive post-war reconstruction. Hariri invested heavily in rebuilding Beirut downtown, developing infrastructure. His economic policies brought growth but also massive debt. Hariri was Lebanon's most influential politician post-war.

events.title: Israel Withdraws from South Lebanon
events.description: Under pressure from Hezbollah's continued resistance, Israel unilaterally withdrew from South Lebanon, ending 22 years of occupation. South Lebanon Army collapsed. Hezbollah claimed resistance victory, prestige soared. But Shebaa Farms disputed area remains contentious.

events.title: Cedar Revolution
events.description: In February 2005, former PM Hariri was assassinated by car bomb in Beirut, Syria widely accused. Hundreds of thousands of Lebanese took to streets protesting Syrian occupation. Under international pressure, Syria was forced to withdraw troops, ending 29-year occupation. But Syria maintained influence through Hezbollah and allies.

events.title: 2006 Lebanon War
events.description: Hezbollah cross-border attack and kidnapping of Israeli soldiers triggered 34-day war. Israel heavily bombed South Lebanon, Beirut suburbs and infrastructure. Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets at Israel. War killed about 1200 Lebanese and 160 Israelis. After ceasefire, UN peacekeepers increased, Lebanese army deployed to south.

events.title: Beirut Clashes
events.description: Government decision to shut down Hezbollah's telecommunications network and remove airport security chief (Hezbollah ally) triggered Hezbollah takeover of West Beirut, clashing with pro-government militias. This was worst violence since civil war. Qatar mediation led to Doha Agreement, forming national unity government.

events.title: Syrian Civil War Spillover
events.description: Syrian civil war deeply impacted Lebanon. Over 1 million Syrian refugees fled to Lebanon. Hezbollah openly intervened supporting Assad. Lebanon divided into pro/anti-Assad camps. Sectarian tensions intensified, sporadic clashes and bombings occurred. Lebanon's economy and infrastructure overwhelmed.

events.title: Hariri Resignation Drama
events.description: PM Hariri suddenly announced resignation from Saudi Arabia, accusing Iran and Hezbollah of dominating Lebanon. Widely seen as Saudi pressure. After international intervention, Hariri returned to Lebanon, withdrew resignation. This incident exposed deep Gulf-Iran rivalry in Lebanon.

events.title: October Revolution Protests
events.description: Government's proposed WhatsApp tax triggered massive nationwide protests. Hundreds of thousands demanded political class resignation, end to corruption and sectarianism. Protesters chanted 'all of them means all of them', demanding entire ruling elite departure. Hariri resigned but crisis continued.

events.title: Debt Default
events.description: Lebanon defaulted on foreign debt for first time, failing to pay $1.2 billion Eurobond. This marked Lebanon's economic collapse. Lebanese pound lost 90% value, banks imposed capital controls, savings became inaccessible. Hyperinflation and unemployment soared.

events.title: Beirut Port Explosion
events.description: 2,750 tons of ammonium nitrate stored in Beirut port warehouse exploded, killing 218, injuring over 7,000, leaving 300,000 homeless. Explosion destroyed port and surrounding areas, blast wave swept Beirut. This disaster stemmed from corruption and incompetence. Explosion exacerbated economic and political crisis, triggering new protests.

events.title: Economic Collapse
events.description: Lebanon experienced unprecedented economic collapse, called one of world's worst since 1850s. Currency lost over 98% value, GDP plummeted 40%, over 80% population fell into poverty. Banking system collapsed, electricity nearly ceased, medicine and fuel shortages. Political elite blocked reforms. IMF bailout stalled. Brain drain intensified, many Lebanese fled abroad.

events.title: Ongoing Crises
events.description: Lebanon continues mired in multiple crises: economic collapse, political stalemate, rampant corruption, infrastructure collapse. Hezbollah-Israel clashes escalate on southern border due to Gaza war. Lebanese struggle to survive, many with only hours of electricity daily. International aid blocked by political reform demands. Lebanon, once the Middle East's jewel, now an example of failed state, future uncertain.
